objective: Starting as a low-privileged IAM user, abuse iam:PassRole + lambda:CreateFunction to run code as an administrator role — then fix the policy so the path no longer works.
successCriteria: You identified the role that carries AdministratorAccess and can be passed to Lambda
You retrieved the production secret using the escalated identity
You rewrote the intern policy so PassRole is limited to a safe role, for Lambda only
hints: Lambda runs your code under an IAM role. Who is allowed to hand a role to Lambda?
List the roles in the account and look at what policies are attached to each. One of them is far too powerful.
Create a function that uses DataPipelineRole as its --role, invoke it, then read the secret prod/master-key.

range.scenario: A contractor's access key for the IAM user `dev-intern` leaked in a public Git repo, and you have it. The intern is only supposed to build and test small Lambda functions, so nothing about the policy looks dangerous at first glance. Your job: work out whether a user who can create Lambda functions and pass ONE role can reach administrator in account 111122223333, prove it by reading the production secret `prod/master-key`, and then fix the policy so the path is closed. Use the terminal to explore like you would with the AWS CLI; the artifacts show you what the cloud console would.

tasks.prompt: Looking at dev-intern-policy.json, which combination of permissions gives this user a path to a more powerful identity?
options: iam:List* and iam:Get* — read-only IAM access
lambda:CreateFunction + iam:PassRole on a role that is more privileged than the user
tasks.explanation: Creating a Lambda function lets you run code, and iam:PassRole lets you choose which role that code runs as. If the passable role is more powerful than you, running code as it IS privilege escalation. The read-only and identity calls only help you discover the path.

tasks.prompt: Use the terminal to list the roles and their attached policies. What is the name of the role that has AdministratorAccess?
tasks.explanation: DataPipelineRole carries AdministratorAccess, and its trust policy lets lambda.amazonaws.com assume it — so anyone who can pass it to Lambda can run admin code. A 'temporary' broad policy on a service role is one of the most common real-world causes of escalation.

tasks.prompt: Perform the escalation: create a Lambda function that uses the powerful role, invoke it, then read the secret prod/master-key. Paste the flag.
tasks.explanation: The function ran with DataPipelineRole's administrator permissions, so it could attach AdministratorAccess to your own user — after which Secrets Manager access worked. dev-intern never needed iam:AttachUserPolicy itself; PassRole was enough.

tasks.prompt: Which single change to the policy best breaks the escalation while still letting the intern deploy Lambda functions?
options: Limit iam:PassRole to a low-privilege role, and only for the Lambda service
Add s3:* so the intern has less reason to use Lambda
tasks.explanation: The dangerous permission is the unrestricted PassRole of a powerful role. Scoping PassRole to a safe role (and conditioning it on iam:PassedToService) keeps the intern productive while removing the path. Removing Invoke alone wouldn't help — Lambda can be triggered other ways.

tasks.prompt: Fix dev-intern's policy. The intern must still create/invoke Lambda functions and pass SandboxLambdaRole to Lambda — but must NOT be able to pass DataPipelineRole, or pass any role to a service other than Lambda.

tests.name: Can still pass SandboxLambdaRole to Lambda

tasks.explanation: Two controls close the hole: Resource restricts WHICH role can be passed, and the iam:PassedToService condition restricts WHICH service it may be passed to. Together they implement least privilege for PassRole.

tasks.prompt: In one word or phrase: which AWS-managed policy attached to DataPipelineRole is the root cause that made passing it so dangerous?
tasks.explanation: PassRole is only as dangerous as the role being passed. Giving a service role AdministratorAccess 'to make it work' turns every PassRole grant for that role into an admin grant. Scope service roles to exactly what the workload needs.

takeaways: iam:PassRole is a privilege-escalation primitive: the risk is the power of the role being passed, not the permission name.
Always scope PassRole to specific role ARNs and add iam:PassedToService so the role can only go to the intended service.
Audit service roles for AdministratorAccess or wildcard policies — they turn small permissions into account takeover.
